query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Minor boron additions (0.1–0.2 at%) to a eutectic high-entropy alloy, followed by homogenization at 1100–1200 °C and controlled cooling, will simultaneously increase yield strength and tensile ductility at room temperature compared with the undoped lamellar-colony baseline.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase (fcc/B2) lamellar colonies known to exhibit limited ductility at room temperature.
generation.intervention: Add 0.1–0.2 at% boron to the base composition via vacuum induction melting, then perform homogenization at 1100–1200 °C, followed by controlled cooling.
generation.conditions: Standard ingot casting with vacuum induction melting; precisely controlled boron addition (0.1–0.2 at%), homogenize at 1100–1200 °C for sufficient time (2–4 hours) to ensure uniform distribution; terminate with a mild cooling schedule that preserves lamellar spacing.
generation.structural_mediator: Boron segregation to internal lamellar boundaries, reducing boundary energy and mitigating microcrack initiation loci.
generation.mechanism: Interface strengthening and enhanced interfacial cohesion from boron segregation reduce early crack propagation, while slight solid-solution strengthening from boron further raises yield strength, together improving both ductility and strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified lamellar microstructure, yield strength increases by about 10–20% at room temperature and tensile ductility improves by ~5–15 additional percentage points of elongation before fracture.
generation.baseline: A lamellar, dual-phase eutectic HEA without boron, known to microcrack easily in tension at room temperature and exhibit limited ductility.
generation.boundary: Boron content above 0.2 at% may lead to additional phases or excessive segregation causing embrittlement; sub-0.1 at% addition may not significantly improve mechanical properties.
generation.uncertainty: Though boundary doping strategies have proven effective in other alloy systems, quantitative boron-solubility limits and full synergy with multi-principal-element compositions remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two alloy batches (0.1–0.2 at% B vs. 0 at% B) under identical conditions, then compare their as-homogenized and heat-treated microstructures and mechanical properties via uniaxial tensile tests at room temperature.
measurements: Chemical composition (via X-ray fluorescence or spark optical emission spectrometry)
Boundary chemistry (atom probe tomography or TEM-EDX)
Room-temperature tensile stress-strain behavior (yield strength, fracture strength, and ductility)
Fractography (SEM) to evaluate crack initiation sites
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If boron addition fails to increase both yield strength and elongation at failure relative to the undoped baseline, or if microcracking remains unchanged despite confirmed boron segregation, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Materials with high performance both at room and elevated temperatures are very attractive for a wide range of critical applications, potentially for aero-engine and fusion reactors [1] – [4] . For decades, ultra-strong, ductile, and heat-resistant materials have long been sought by the materials community, such as tungsten-based heavy alloys and nickel-based superalloys [3] , [5] . However, achieving alloys with an ultrahigh strength (>2 GPa) and a sufficient ductility (>10%) has presented a long-standing challenge. This has spurred significant research into metallurgical strategies to tailor microstructures for improved properties. One classical design paradigm is utilizing dilute concentrations of alloying elements, such as Re, Ti, and Cr, to improve the properties of W-based alloys; however, the “strength-ductility trade-off” has proven to be difficult to be solved with such single principal-element alloy systems due to the problem of brittle W-enriched phases with body-centered cubic (bcc) structures [5] , [6] . chosen.lever: boron doping of eutectic high-entropy alloy
chosen.technique: vacuum induction melting plus controlled homogenization
chosen.conditions: 0.1–0.2 at% B added to the standard alloy feedstock, homogenized at 1100–1200°C, followed by a standard cooling protocol
chosen.why: Although prior microstructural and processing strategies have not resolved the room-temperature brittleness of dual-phase lamellar high-entropy alloys, targeted grain-boundary doping is a well-established method for reducing interfacial decohesion. Boron segregates to internal boundaries, lowers their energy, and impedes microcrack formation. This approach can simultaneously increase strength (via slight solute strengthening) and improve ductility (by inhibiting crack initiation at lamellar interfaces), and it is straightforward to implement via standard ingot metallurgy procedures.
